title: Meta Q2 revenue beats at $60.8B, but AI capex and free-cash-flow drop drag the stock down 7%
subtitle: Zuckerberg raised the low end of full-year 2026 AI capex guidance to $130B and hinted Meta may sell cloud capacity to third parties — a strategy shift markets are still digesting.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta reported second-quarter 2026 results on July 29, posting revenue of $60.8 billion, up 28% year-over-year and ahead of the $59.5 billion consensus. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $6.18, missing analyst estimates of roughly $7.13. Net income fell 14% to $15.8 billion, weighed down by $2.4 billion in legal charges and $1.18 billion in severance from the May 2026 layoffs. Capital expenditures for the quarter hit $31.08 billion, and Meta raised the low end of its full-year 2026 capex guidance from $125 billion to $130 billion, keeping the top of the range at $145 billion. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading.

The number that mattered most on the call was not revenue growth or the EPS miss but free cash flow, which was crushed by the pace of the AI buildout. Mark Zuckerberg also used the call to signal that Meta may begin selling excess data-center capacity to third parties — a first step toward operating a cloud business alongside Google, Microsoft, and Amazon. That is a structural shift, not a minor product note: Meta has spent two decades framing its infrastructure as pure internal cost, and the pivot only makes financial sense if AI workloads keep expanding faster than the ad business can absorb.

Meta's numbers land in the middle of a big-tech earnings week that has become a referendum on the AI capex cycle. Alphabet's Q2 already flagged a $205 billion capex target, Microsoft's Q4 FY26 report the same evening raised its FY27 capex to roughly $175 billion, and analysts now expect the four US hyperscalers to spend a combined $725 billion-plus on infrastructure this calendar year. The pattern is consistent — revenue keeps growing, but the ratio of AI investment to reported profit is compressing margins across the group, and investors are punishing the companies that can't clearly show a return path.

For learners: watch the free-cash-flow line, not the headline revenue number, when reading hyperscaler earnings this cycle. Revenue can grow while a company is quietly hollowing itself out to fund infrastructure, and cash flow is the first place that shows. The same discipline applies to smaller AI companies — a startup can post impressive top-line growth while burning through cash on compute, and the burn rate tells you more about survivability than the ARR chart in the pitch deck.
